outcomes.text: State the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe how particles are separated, arranged and moving in solids, liquids and gases.

subtopics.title: Changes of state and gas behaviour

outcomes.text: Describe melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing as changes of state.
Describe how temperature and pressure change the volume of a gas.
Explain changes of state with kinetic particle theory, including heating and cooling curves.
Explain with kinetic particle theory how temperature and pressure affect gas volume.
Describe and explain diffusion using kinetic particle theory.
Explain how relative molecular mass affects the rate at which gases diffuse.
Describe how elements, compounds and mixtures differ.

topics.title: 2.2 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Describe the atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells.
State the relative charges and masses of a proton, neutron and electron.
Define proton (atomic) number as the number of protons in the nucleus.
Define mass (nucleon) number as the total of protons and neutrons.

subtopics.title: Electron shells and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Work out electronic configurations of atoms and ions with proton numbers 1 to 20.
Link full outer shells, group number and period number to electron arrangement.
Define isotopes as atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
Read and write symbols for atoms and ions showing mass and proton numbers.
Explain why isotopes of an element share chemical properties.
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope masses and abundances.
Describe how positive ions (cations) and negative ions (anions) form.
State that an ionic bond is the strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Describe ionic bond formation between Group I and Group VII elements using dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe ionic bond formation between other metals and non-metals using dot-and-cross diagrams.

subtopics.title: Structure and properties of ionic compounds

outcomes.text: Describe the high melting points and conductivity (molten or aqueous, not solid) of ionic compounds.
Describe the giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions.
Explain ionic compound properties using structure and bonding.
State that a covalent bond is a shared electron pair giving noble gas configurations.
Describe covalent bonding in H2, Cl2, H2O, CH4, NH3 and HCl with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe covalent bonding in CH3OH, C2H4, O2, CO2 and N2 with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe the low melting and boiling points and poor conductivity of simple molecular compounds.
Explain these properties using weak intermolecular forces and structure.
Describe the giant covalent structures of graphite and diamond.
Relate the structures of graphite and diamond to their uses as lubricant, electrode and cutting tool.
Describe the giant covalent structure of silicon(IV) oxide.
Explain why diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have similar properties.
Describe metallic bonding as attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Explain metals' electrical conductivity, malleability and ductility from their structure.
State the formulae of the elements and compounds named in the syllabus.
Define the molecular formula of a compound.
Deduce a simple compound's formula from atoms in a model or diagram.
Define the empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms or ions.
Deduce an ionic compound's formula from ions in a model or from their charges.
Write word equations and symbol equations with state symbols.
Write symbol equations with state symbols, including ionic equations.
Deduce a full symbol equation with state symbols from given information.

topics.title: 3.2 Relative masses of atoms and molecules

outcomes.text: Describe relative atomic mass as the average isotope mass compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.
Define relative molecular (formula) mass as the sum of relative atomic masses.
Calculate reacting masses in simple proportions without using moles.

topics.title: 3.3 The mole and the Avogadro constant

subtopics.title: The mole and amount of substance

outcomes.text: State that the mole is the unit of amount and holds 6.02 x 10^23 particles.
Use amount = mass / molar mass to find amount, mass, molar mass or particle numbers.
Use the molar gas volume of 24 dm3 at r.t.p. in gas calculations.
State that concentration is measured in g/dm3 or mol/dm3.
Calculate reacting masses, limiting reactants, gas volumes and solution concentrations, converting cm3 and dm3.
Use titration data to find moles of solute, concentration or volume.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulae from data.
Calculate percentage yield, percentage composition by mass and percentage purity.
Define electrolysis as breaking down a molten or aqueous ionic compound with electric current.
Identify the anode, cathode and electrolyte in a simple electrolytic cell.
Describe charge transfer: electron flow, gain and loss of electrons at electrodes, ion movement.
State that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-hydrogen non-metals at the anode.
Identify products and observations in electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, concentrated brine and dilute sulfuric acid.
Identify products in electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon and copper electrodes.
Predict products at each electrode for a molten binary compound.
Predict products for halide compounds in dilute or concentrated aqueous solution.
Write ionic half-equations for oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
State that electroplating improves appearance and corrosion resistance.
Describe how metals are electroplated.
State that a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell makes electricity with water as the only product.
Compare hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells with petrol engines in vehicles.
State that exothermic reactions release thermal energy and raise surrounding temperature.
State that endothermic reactions absorb thermal energy and lower surrounding temperature.
State that enthalpy change, delta H, is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Define activation energy as the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.
Draw and label pathway diagrams showing reactants, products, delta H and activation energy.
Explain enthalpy change using bond breaking (endothermic) and bond making (exothermic).
Calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from bond energies.
Identify physical and chemical changes and describe how they differ.
Describe how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts change rate.
State that a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is unchanged at the end.
State that a catalyst lowers the activation energy.
Describe collision theory: particles per volume, collision frequency, kinetic energy, activation energy.
Describe and explain the effect of each rate factor using collision theory.
Describe practical methods for rate: change in mass, gas formation.
Interpret data and graphs from rate experiments.
Evaluate practical methods for investigating rate.
State that some reactions are reversible, shown by the symbol for reversibility.
Describe how heating and adding water reverse hydrated copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride changes.
State that equilibrium in a closed system means equal forward and reverse rates and constant concentrations.
Predict and explain how temperature, pressure, concentration and catalyst affect equilibrium position.
State the Haber process equation for making ammonia.
State the sources of hydrogen (methane) and nitrogen (air).
State the Haber process conditions: 450 C, 200 atm, iron catalyst.
State the equation for converting sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.
State the sources of sulfur dioxide and oxygen.
State the Contact process conditions: 450 C, 2 atm, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
Explain the chosen conditions for both processes using rate, equilibrium, safety and economics.
Use Roman numerals to show oxidation numbers in compounds.
Define redox as simultaneous oxidation and reduction.
Define oxidation and reduction as gain and loss of oxygen, and identify them.
Define oxidation and reduction as loss and gain of electrons, or change in oxidation number.
Identify redox from electron transfer.
Apply the rules for oxidation numbers to identify redox reactions.
Identify redox by colour changes with acidified potassium manganate(VII) or potassium iodide.
Define an oxidising agent as a substance that oxidises another and is itself reduced.
Define a reducing agent as a substance that reduces another and is itself oxidised.
Identify oxidising and reducing agents in redox reactions.

topics.title: 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases

outcomes.text: Describe acid reactions with metals, bases and carbonates.
Describe the effect of acids on litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that bases are metal oxides or hydroxides and alkalis are soluble bases.
Describe base reactions with acids and ammonium salts.
Describe the effect of alkalis on litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that acids contain H+ ions and alkalis contain OH- ions in water.
Compare acidity, alkalinity and neutrality with universal indicator paper and pH.
Describe neutralisation of an acid by an alkali to form water.
Define acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
Define strong acids as fully dissociated and weak acids as partially dissociated.
State that hydrochloric acid is strong, shown by its dissociation equation.
State that ethanoic acid is weak, shown by its reversible equation.
Classify oxides as acidic or basic using metallic and non-metallic character.
Describe amphoteric oxides as reacting with both acids and bases.
Classify aluminium oxide and zinc oxide as amphoteric.
Describe preparing and purifying soluble salts from an acid with an alkali, metal, base or carbonate.
Describe the general solubility rules for common salts.
Describe making insoluble salts by precipitation.
Define hydrated and anhydrous substances.
Define water of crystallisation, including CuSO4.5H2O and CoCl2.6H2O.
Describe the Periodic Table as periods and groups in order of proton number.
Describe the change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period.
Relate group number to the charge on ions formed.
Explain similar chemical properties within a group using electronic configuration.
Use an element's position to predict its properties.
Identify trends in groups from given information.
Describe lithium, sodium and potassium as soft metals, with trends down the group.
Predict properties of other Group I elements from given information.
Describe the halogens as diatomic non-metals with trends down the group.
State the appearance of chlorine, bromine and iodine at r.t.p.
Describe and explain halogen displacement reactions with halide ions.
Predict properties of other Group VII elements.
Describe transition elements as dense, high-melting metals with coloured compounds and catalytic uses.
Describe their ions as having variable oxidation numbers, such as iron(II) and iron(III).
Describe noble gases as unreactive monatomic gases, explained by electronic configuration.
Compare physical properties of metals and non-metals.
Describe reactions of metals with dilute acids, water and oxygen.
Describe uses of aluminium and copper based on their physical properties.
Describe an alloy as a mixture of a metal with other elements, such as brass and stainless steel.
State that alloys can be harder and stronger than pure metals.
Describe uses of alloys based on properties, such as stainless steel cutlery.
Identify alloys from structure diagrams.
Explain alloy hardness: different-sized atoms stop layers sliding.
State the order of the reactivity series.
Describe reactions of metals with cold water, steam and dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain them using the series.
Deduce an order of reactivity from experimental results.
Describe reactivity through tendency to form positive ions and displacement reactions.
Explain the apparent unreactivity of aluminium through its oxide layer.
State the conditions needed for iron to rust.
State common barrier methods: painting, greasing, plastic coating.
Describe how barrier methods stop rusting by excluding oxygen or water.
Describe zinc galvanising as barrier and sacrificial protection.
Explain sacrificial protection with the reactivity series and electron loss.
Describe how a metal's reactivity relates to how easily it is extracted from its ore.
Describe iron extraction from hematite in the blast furnace.
State the symbol equations for extracting iron.
State that bauxite is the main aluminium ore and aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.
Describe aluminium extraction, including cryolite, anode replacement and electrode half-equations.
Describe water tests with anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride and anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
Describe testing purity with melting and boiling points.
Explain why distilled water, not tap water, is used in practical chemistry.
State substances water from natural sources may contain.
State which of these substances are beneficial.
State which of these substances are harmful.
Describe domestic water treatment: sedimentation, filtration, carbon, chlorination.
State that ammonium salts and nitrates are used as fertilisers.
Describe NPK fertilisers supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
State the composition of clean, dry air.
State the sources of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, particulates, methane, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide.
State the adverse effects of each of these pollutants.
Describe how carbon dioxide and methane cause global warming.
State and explain strategies to reduce climate change and acid rain.
Explain how nitrogen oxides form in car engines and are removed by catalytic converters.
Describe photosynthesis as carbon dioxide and water making glucose and oxygen.
State the word equation for photosynthesis.
State the symbol equation for photosynthesis.
Draw and interpret displayed formulae showing all atoms and bonds.
State that a structural formula unambiguously shows how atoms are arranged.
Define structural isomers as compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.
Write and interpret general formulae for alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Identify a functional group as the part that decides chemical properties.
State that a homologous series is a family with the same functional group.
Describe the general characteristics of a homologous series.
State what saturated and unsaturated compounds are.
Name and draw methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid and reaction products from 11.4 to 11.7.
Identify compound type from names ending -ane, -ene, -ol or -oic acid, or from formulae.
Name and draw unbranched alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids up to four carbons.
Name and draw unbranched esters made from alcohols and acids up to four carbons.
Name coal, natural gas and petroleum as fossil fuels.
Name methane as the main constituent of natural gas.
State that hydrocarbons contain only hydrogen and carbon.
State that petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
Describe separating petroleum into fractions by fractional distillation.
Describe how fraction properties change up the column.
Name the uses of each petroleum fraction.
State that alkanes have single covalent bonds and are saturated hydrocarbons.
Describe alkanes as generally unreactive, apart from combustion and substitution with chlorine.
State what a substitution reaction is.
Describe alkane substitution with chlorine as photochemical, and draw monosubstituted products.
State that alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and are unsaturated.
Describe making alkenes and hydrogen by cracking larger alkanes.
Describe the reasons for cracking larger alkanes.
Describe the bromine water test for unsaturation.
State that an addition reaction forms only one product.
Describe alkene addition with bromine, hydrogen and steam, and draw the products.
Describe making ethanol by fermentation and by steam addition to ethene.
Describe the combustion of ethanol.
State the uses of ethanol as a solvent and fuel.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of the two manufacturing methods.
Describe ethanoic acid reacting with metals, bases and carbonates, naming the salts.
Describe forming ethanoic acid by oxidising ethanol, including vinegar production.
Describe an acid and an alcohol reacting with an acid catalyst to form an ester.
Define polymers as large molecules built from monomers.
Describe forming poly(ethene) by addition polymerisation.
Identify repeat units and linkages in addition polymers.
Deduce an addition polymer's repeat unit from its alkene and vice versa.
State that plastics are made from polymers.
Describe how plastic properties affect disposal.
Describe plastic problems: landfill, ocean accumulation, toxic gases when burned.
State that PET can be converted back to monomers and re-polymerised.
Deduce condensation polymer structures from monomers: polyamides and polyesters.
Describe the differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Describe and draw the structures of nylon and PET.
Describe proteins as natural polyamides made of amino acids.
Describe and draw the structure of a protein chain.
Name apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume.
Suggest advantages and disadvantages of methods and apparatus.
Describe solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue and filtrate.
Describe an acid-base titration with a burette, volumetric pipette and indicator.
Describe finding the end-point with an indicator.
Describe separating soluble coloured substances by paper chromatography.
Interpret chromatograms to identify unknowns and judge purity.
Describe separating colourless substances using a locating agent.
State and use the Rf equation.
Describe and explain separation by solvent, filtration, crystallisation and distillation.
Suggest suitable techniques given information about the substances.
Assess purity using melting and boiling points.
Describe tests for carbonate, halide, nitrate, sulfate and sulfite ions.
Describe tests with sodium hydroxide and ammonia for aluminium, ammonium, calcium, chromium(III), copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) and zinc ions.
Describe flame tests for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, barium and copper(II).
Describe tests for ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur dioxide.
